newsitem.title: JAPAN: U.S., Japan to conclude deal on Okinawa bases.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan to conclude deal on Okinawa bases.

text.p: The United States and Japan plan to conclude talks on reducing U.S. military bases on Okinawa during high-level talks on Monday in an effort to settle an issue thrust into prominence by the rape of a Okinawan schoolgirl.

U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry and U.S. Ambassador to Japan Walter Mondale are to meet Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda and Defence Minister Fumio Kyuma in Tokyo to conclude the Okinawa talks, Foreign Ministry officials said.
The two sides are expected to seal an agreement on closing 11 U.S. bases and military facilities on southern Japan's Okinawa island, the ministry officials said.

The subtropical island, about 1,000 km (625 miles) southwest of Tokyo, is home to three-quarters of the U.S. military facilities and about half of the 47,000 U.S. military personnel stationed in Japan, although it constitutes less than one percent of the country's land area.
The rape of an Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen in September 1994 triggered a public outcry against the huge U.S. military presence on the island.
Two years later in September 1996, Okinawans overwhelmingly passed a provincial referendum demanding the streamlining of U.S. bases on the island.
The key issue at stake is the replacement of a U.S. Marine Corps helicopter base at Futemma, located in an urban area in southern Okinawa.
Japan has proposed erecting an off-shore "floating" heliport somewhere off the coast of Okinawa, but most local governments on Okinawa have opposed the idea.
In the Tokyo talks, the two sides were expected to postpone a decision on where they would build a new heliport and instead agree to set up a new committee to continue discussions.

In talks with President Bill Clinton in Manila last week, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto agreed to settle the Okinawan issue during Monday's talks so the two sides can move ahead on strategic issues, including talks for drafting a new set of guidelines for Japan to support the U.S. military.

The new set of guidelines will replace the current ones under the 1960 U.S.-Japan Security Treaty, which bans Japan from supplying the U.S. military during wartime, except when Japan itself has been invaded.
The new guidelines were expected to address the question of Japan's military support in future regional conflicts, such as a possible conflict with North Korea.
Talks on the guidelines are expected to last another year.
Besides the guidelines, the two sides were also expected to begin discussions on Japan's possible participation in a U.S.-led plan to deploy missiles to shoot down incoming ballistic missiles.

Japan's Defence Ministry has studied the plan, called Theatre Missile Defence (TMD), for two years. It would be primarily aimed at containing possible missile threats from countries like North Korea, which have been test-firing ballistic missiles in recent years.
